title: Omitted variables in linear models
dek: Leave a relevant regressor out and OLS estimates a different functional — the projection onto the columns you kept. Call that bias only after you name the target.
story: Suppose the long regression is Y = Xβ + Zγ + ε with E[ε | X,Z] = 0. The short regression of Y on X only estimates δ in Y = Xδ + u, where δ = β + (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ Z γ in the sample (and a population analogue with covariances). The extra term is omitted-variable bias for β if β was the target.

If the target was the predictive projection onto X, there is no bias — you got that projection. The word “bias” smuggles a target. In a genomics lab this is the difference between “association with lineage” and “effect of a mutation holding lineage fixed.”

The sign of the bias is the product of (how Z enters Y) and (how Z correlates with X). A resistance mutation that tracks lineage will look like a lineage effect in a short model, and like a mutation effect in a long model, and like neither if you still omitted treatment history.
deepTitle: Algebra, DAGs, and what OLS cannot see
deep: Scalar formula: bias = γ · (coefficient of Z on X). If γ = 0 (Z does not enter the mean of Y) or Z is uncorrelated with X, the short coefficient equals β. Randomisation of X is the design way to force the second.

Including Z can also be wrong: if Z is a collider or a mediator you wanted to leave in the total effect, the long regression estimates a different causal functional. Omitted-variable folklore that “more controls are always better” is false in DAG language — see the causal plates.
Measurement error in X, not omission of Z, is a different bias (usually attenuation for classical error). Sandwich SEs do not fix either.

In GLMs the algebra is not exactly (XᵀX)⁻¹ XᵀZγ, but the same moral holds: the coefficient is defined by the score of the model you fit. Nested LRTs compare those models; they do not tell you which target is scientific.

visual.caption: The omitted-variable path: X is correlated with Z, Z shifts Y, and a short regression of Y on X absorbs part of γ into δ. Randomising X would cut the X—Z association; controlling Z in the mean is the regression move, when Z is a confounder not a collider.

example.title: gyrA and lineage
example.setup: Short logit or OLS-on-linear-probability: FQ-R ~ gyrA QRDR mutation. Long: add lineage L2. Mutation is more common in L2, and L2 has higher FQ-R for additional reasons (treatment history, other alleles).

steps.title: Auxiliary
steps.body: Regress the mutation on L2: π > 0. The omitted lineage coefficient γ > 0 on FQ-R. Short mutation coefficient is inflated relative to the long-regression β.

steps.title: Name the target
steps.body: If the scientific question is “does this mutation shift MIC holding lineage and treatment fixed?”, the long model is closer (and still not a DAG-complete causal model). If the question is “what is the predictive association in the population?”, the short model is a legitimate projection.

steps.title: LRT is not the referee of targets
steps.body: A nested LRT will likely reject the short model. That says lineage earns likelihood, not that β is the causal effect of gyrA.

example.takeaway: Write δ = β + πγ, then write the sentence for β you actually wanted.

check.prompt: Omitted-variable bias for the included coefficient is zero if:
choices: The omitted Z does not enter the mean of Y, or Z is uncorrelated with included X
You always add every measured covariate
check.answer: The omitted Z does not enter the mean of Y, or Z is uncorrelated with included X
check.why: γ = 0 or π = 0. Sandwich does not remove mean bias. Adding colliders can create bias.

whyWrong.n > 30: Asymptotics do not cancel a missing confounder.

check.answer: Omitted-variable bias for β needs Z to be associated with the included regressor
check.why: If π = 0, short and long coefficients agree even when γ ≠ 0 (Z is a pure noise predictor of Y).
